newsitem.title: CHINA: China reschedules next satellite launch.
newsitem.headline: China reschedules next satellite launch.

text.p: China has rescheduled its next satellite launch, originally planned for this week, with the new launch date tentatively set for May 13, industry sources said on Friday.

The global satellite insurance business is watching warily to see if China's coming satellite launch is successful after the failure of its last two launch attempts in 1996, apparently due to problems with the Long March launch rocket, the sources said.
The next satellite due to go into orbit is the Dongfanghong-3 domestic communications satellite to be launched using a Long March 3a rocket, produced by the China Great Wall Industries Corp.
"The launch was supposed to be on May 5 but I understand it has been postponed until May 13," an industry source said. "They are making sure they have a successful launch."

An official at the China Pacific Insurance Company in Shanghai, one of the insurers of the Dongfanghong (East is Red) satellite, said it should have been launched by now, based on their understanding of the schedule.
He said the company had received no notification on the current status of the launch.
An official with the China Aerospace Group in Beijing, which is handling the satellite launch, said the launch was scheduled for May and that there had been no delay.
"We are waiting for the right conditions for the launch," the official said. "It could be within the next few days."
Insurance premiums for China satellite launches are substantially higher than the international average due to problems with the Long March launcher, the insurance source said.
"Chinese premiums are definitely higher, perhaps 27 percent or more, whereas elsewhere they are lower," he said.
A successful launch of the Dongfanghong-3 satellite, originally scheduled for launch late last year, is necessary to restore confidence.
"If it doesn't go, or if there is problem on its way up, a lot of people will be very nervous," the source said.
A second Chinese satellite, the Fengyun-2 weather satellite, is due for launch in late June or early July.
China Aerospace is also scheduled to launch at least three international satellites this year -- a Philippine telecommunications satellite, Apstar IIR and Chinasat-1.
All have been delayed due to the two 1996 failures.
The Intelsat 708 satellite, worth $230 million, was lost in February 1996 when the launcher veered off course immediately after lift-off and exploded, killing six people.
In August 1996, another satellite was stranded in a useless orbit.
Solving the launch problem has huge implications for China and for the global satellite launch industry, given the fast growth in demand for satellite launches.
China Aerospace officials have said they plan to use the Long March rocket to launch more than 30 satellites for other countries in the next four years.
China has launched a total of 48 satellites, including 43 launches using Long March rockets.
"The Chinese want to be seen as leaders in the business, and we all want them to succeed, but it will take two successful launches in a row to do it," said the industry source.
